observations: The source problem asks for positive integers a,b,c with 3*sqrt(cbrt(5)-cbrt(4)) = cbrt(a)+cbrt(b)-cbrt(c).
The failed trajectory guessed small integers numerically and concluded a=9,b=2,c=12, but its own exact check did not verify the identity.
A deterministic approach is to search over a bounded range of positive integers and verify the identity using high-precision arithmetic, then return the sum a+b+c for the first exact match.
The computation should be parameterized by the two radicands inside the outer square root and the outer multiplier, plus a search bound, so it generalizes beyond this instance.

bound.description: Maximum value for a,b,c in the search

multiplier.description: Outer multiplier of the square root on the left side

p.description: First radicand under the inner cube root on the left side

q.description: Second radicand under the inner cube root on the left side

procedure_plan: Define parameters p, q (positive integers under cube roots), multiplier m (positive integer), and bound N. Compute target = m*sqrt(cbrt(p)-cbrt(q)) using high-precision decimal arithmetic. Iterate a,b,c from 1 to N; for each triple compute value = cbrt(a)+cbrt(b)-cbrt(c) in the same precision and check |value-target| < tolerance. Collect all matching triples; if exactly one, return its sum a+b+c; if multiple, return the minimal sum; if none, return null. Use tolerance small enough (e.g. 1e-40) to avoid false positives from floating point, and optionally confirm with an exact algebraic check by cubing/squaring both sides symbolically when feasible.
uncertainty: The main uncertainty is whether the true a,b,c lie within the chosen bound N and whether floating-point tolerance is tight enough to uniquely identify the triple. If multiple triples match numerically, an exact symbolic verification (comparing coefficients in the basis of cube roots) is needed to disambiguate. Also, the identity may admit a different representation than the one guessed, so the search must be broad enough.
